desc:
You may delete any characters from the string s (not necessarily neighbouring ones). The remaining characters keep their order. You want the remaining string to be self-cancelling: it can be reduced to the empty string by repeatedly deleting two neighbouring equal letters.

Return the minimum number of characters you must delete. Deleting every character is always allowed, so an answer exists.

Example: 'abccba' needs 0 deletions (cc, then bb, then aa cancel). For 'abcab' the answer is 3: keeping only the two a's (or the two b's) is the best possible.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: A string is self-cancelling exactly when its letters can be matched in equal pairs so that no two pairs cross (pairs may be nested or side by side). So you want the largest such matching among the letters of s.
Use interval dynamic programming: f(i, j) is the largest number of letters of s[i..j) that can be matched in this way. Look at the first letter of the interval.
Either the first letter is not used: f(i + 1, j). Or it is paired with a later equal letter at position k: 2 + f(i + 1, k) + f(k + 1, j). The answer is n - f(0, n).
editorial: Deleting two neighbouring equal letters is a non-crossing pairing: every deleted pair encloses only letters that were removed earlier. Conversely, any set of letter pairs of equal letters that are pairwise non-crossing can be removed from the inside out. So the kept string is self-cancelling if and only if it admits a perfect non-crossing matching of equal letters, and we want the maximum number of letters taking part in such a matching.

Let f(i, j) be that maximum for the half-open interval [i, j). Either position i is unused (f(i + 1, j)), or it is matched to some k with s[k] = s[i], which splits the problem into the inside [i + 1, k) and the outside part [k + 1, j), adding 2 for the pair. Fill the table by decreasing i. There are O(n2) states and O(n) transitions each, so the time is O(n3) with O(n2) space, fine for n ≤ 120.
